analysis.one_liner: Requires big political spenders to disclose their donors and tightens the financial-regulator revolving door.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2016, referred to five House committees, and never received a hearing or a vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill bundles several campaign-finance and ethics reforms into one package. It would require corporations, unions, trade groups, and Super PACs that spend money on elections to report their top donors, put funders' names on political ads, and post that information where shareholders and members can see it. It would tighten rules against candidates coordinating with Super PACs, speed up public reporting of contributions, close a lobbying-registration loophole, and restrict financial-services regulators from leaving government to take industry jobs — or from working on matters that benefit their former employers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would be able to see who is actually paying for the political ads they watch; shareholders, union members, and donors, who would learn how the organizations they own or belong to spend money on politics; and small campaigns, which would no longer compete against Super PAC money that candidates secretly direct.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters tired of hidden election money

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires any corporation, union, tax-exempt group, or Super PAC that spends more than $10,000 on campaign-related communications to file a sworn statement naming each contributor of $10,000 or more during the period.

It extends 'Stand by Your Ad' rules to outside groups, requiring TV ads to show the top five funders, radio ads to name the top two funders, and internet and prerecorded-call ads to carry the same disclosures.

It treats payments for expenditures coordinated with a candidate as illegal contributions, with penalties up to 300% of the excess, and prohibits candidates and federal officeholders from soliciting or directing funds to committees that accept unlimited donations — the structure that lets Super PACs operate alongside campaigns.

It requires political committees to report to the FEC within 48 hours any contributor whose cumulative yearly giving reaches $1,000, and makes Senate candidates file directly with the FEC like House candidates already do.

It replaces the deadlocked six-member Federal Election Commission with a five-member Federal Election Administration with its own chair, general counsel, inspector general, subpoena power, and independent enforcement authority.

It bars financial-services regulators from working on matters that would benefit a former employer or client, restricts regulators from negotiating future private-sector jobs, extends post-employment limits for procurement officers, and tightens rules for federal bank examiners.

It closes the '20-percent lobbying loophole' so people who spend 20% of their time lobbying must register, lengthens the window that counts (two years instead of three months), and requires registered lobbyists to report independent expenditures and electioneering communications of $1,000 or more.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, unions, trade associations, Super PACs, and tax-exempt 'dark money' groups, which would face new reporting, disclosure, and compliance obligations; financial firms, which would face a harder path to hiring former regulators; and lobbying firms, which would face broader registration and spending disclosure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big-money political spenders and financial firms

drawbacks.text: Requiring organizations to name every contributor of $10,000 or more puts individual and group donors' identities into public records, exposing them to public scrutiny and possible retaliation by whoever holds power — the trade-off supporters accept in exchange for transparency.

The 24-hour reporting cycle, the $1,000 thresholds, and the extended window in which communications count as 'electioneering communications' create substantial compliance work for organizations of all sizes, including small nonprofits, from the first day of each election year.

The bill redefines 'independent expenditure' to include communications a 'reasonable person' could interpret as advocacy, a standard that is harder to evade than the current one but also reaches further into political speech, and courts would likely test how far it can go.

Concentrating election enforcement in a single five-member Federal Election Administration, with a powerful chair, trades the current commission's gridlock for a smaller body whose character depends heavily on who appoints its members.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — letting voters see who funds the ads aimed at them, and closing the coordination and revolving-door channels that connect campaigns and industry — is substantial and directly addresses long-standing enforcement gaps. The costs are real but mostly administrative: compliance burdens and loss of donor anonymity, with the donor-exposure trade-off being the strongest good-faith objection. On balance the bill is designed to shift information and power toward voters at the expense of organizations that currently spend without disclosure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees on the day it was introduced; none ever took it up, and it expired with the 114th Congress in January 2017 without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. David Price, a North Carolina Democrat, introduced the We the People Act of 2016 on June 16, 2016, combining several separately authored reform bills into one package.
The same day, the House referred it to five committees — House Administration, Judiciary, Oversight and Government Reform, Financial Services, and Ways and Means.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
Only one House member, a Democrat, cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organizations that spend undisclosed money on elections, the financial-services industry, and lobbying firms avoided all the new disclosure and revolving-door rules; incumbents who rely on Super PAC and dark-money support kept the existing system intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big donors and the financial industry

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call ever tested where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Super PACs and big-money campaign donors
industries.note: The bill forces disclosure of $10,000-plus contributors to campaign-spending groups and criminalizes the candidate coordination that lets Super PACs work in tandem with campaigns. Their interest in operating anonymously runs directly against voters' interest in knowing who is funding election ads.

industries.industry: 'Dark money' nonprofits and trade associations (501(c) groups)
industries.note: These organizations are squarely covered: the bill requires them to report campaign-related disbursements, name top funders in ads, and tell their members. Their current advantage is that voters cannot trace the money, which is exactly what the bill removes.

The bill restricts regulators from working on matters benefiting former employers or clients, limits negotiating future private-sector jobs while in office, and tightens rules for bank examiners. Firms currently benefit from friendly treatment by regulators angling for jobs on their side of the door.

Registration thresholds drop so that far more people doing lobbying work must register, and registered lobbyists must disclose independent expenditures and electioneering communications of $1,000 or more. Their business model depends partly on less visibility, not more.

Unions are covered organizations under the bill, so their political spending would face the same donor-disclosure and ad-funder requirements as corporations'. The rules are symmetrical, but unions spent years building nondisclosure arrangements the bill would unwind.
